extracted.intended_audience: students and competitors preparing for mathematical olympiads / problem-solvers in elementary number theory and combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Solution techniques and problem-solving principles for olympiad-style number theory and combinatorics problems (functional equations, invariants, Pell equations, binomial congruences). The page presents methods, typical invariants, reductions, and counting arguments used to construct or exclude solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use injectivity to restrict possibilities / perform case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit injectivity of a function (or other uniqueness properties) to deduce that certain parameters must take only a few possible values (e.g., from f(k)=g(m)(n) injectivity implies m=0 or m=1 so f(k)=n or n+1987).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine injectivity with functional relations to force limited cases and then rule out or resolve them (pairing/odd-counting contradictions often follow). Example: deducing that arranging 1..1987 in pairs is impossible because 1987 is odd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive monotonicity by algebraic manipulation / substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute special values (often 0 or 1) into a functional equation, subtract relations, and use resulting algebraic identities to prove monotonicity (if m ≥ n then f(m) ≥ f(n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: substituting m=0 and n=0 to get f(m)^2 − f(n)^2 = 2(f(m^2) − f(n^2)), which together with other relations implies f is increasing; then proceed by cases f(0)=0 or 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-splitting on small values to find global form
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the few possible values forced at small arguments (like f(0), f(1), f(2)), then propagate via monotonicity or recurrence to obtain all solutions (e.g., constant solutions or linear forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through the consequences of each small-case choice, use parity/monotonicity/recurrence to extend to all n and discard impossibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit parity / pairing contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Count elements or pairs and use parity (odd/even) to obtain contradictions (e.g., arranging an odd number of integers into disjoint pairs is impossible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in injectivity/pairing arguments: show elements must be partitionable into pairs but total count is odd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization and multiplicativity arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prime factorization and multiplicativity properties (often deduced from the functional equation) to determine values on primes and extend multiplicatively to all integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deducing f(3)=3 from inequalities, using gcd/relatively-prime arguments to get f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for coprime a,b, and then induction across ranges (via rapidly growing sequences) to cover all n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct multiplicative bijections by mapping primes by residue class
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a map g on a restricted domain so g is multiplicative by prescribing images of primes via a bijection between prime residue classes (e.g., map primes of form 3n+1 to 4n+1 and 3n+2 to 4n+3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure well-definedness by parity of occurrences of certain prime types; extend multiplicatively using prime factorization to obtain bijection between sets like 3N0+1 and 4N0+1, then derive original f from g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build solutions using polynomial iteration / orbit decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Define functions via orbits under polynomial maps (compose polynomial P repeatedly), partition integers by their membership in images of iterates, and define f using these orbit indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use P(n)=n^2−19n+99, define g(n) the smallest k such that n not in image of P^k, and use the decomposition to define f so that f(f(n))=P(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary multiplicative transforms
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a complicated functional relation, define an auxiliary function (e.g., g(n)=f(n)+1) that becomes multiplicative or simpler, then solve for g and invert to get f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming f into g multiplicative and then using properties of multiplicative functions and density/limit arguments (using rationals approximating logs) to identify g(n)=n^3 and hence f(n)=n^3−1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick natural invariants (coloring, residues, sums) to obstruct transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a quantity that remains unchanged under allowed moves (coloring parity, sum of coordinates, residues modulo k, weighted sums), and compare initial and target values to show impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: color last square of a path (odd-length path flips color), difference between counts of black and white squares for domino tilings, residue of ∑(Ri+Ci) mod 4 under sign changes, parity of number of pluses in a 2×2 sub-square, weighted sum of coordinates (roots of unity) for bulb problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use difference-of-sums or weighted sums as invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Define weighted linear combinations (e.g., 2x1 + 4x2 + ... modulo 10) whose last digit or residue is invariant under the transformation, then show start/end residues differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to resolve finite-state digit problems: compute the invariant for initial and target configurations; differing residues imply impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group-labeling/product invariants (finite groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Label board squares by elements of a finite group (e.g., Klein four group) so the product of labels covered or uncovered gives an invariant; show no labeling yields required product identity, obstructing covering/tiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: label squares with elements of Klein four group, show product of elements covered by each tile is either a or b with a^2=b^2=e, concluding no covering exists because ax^by=e impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-based product/edge-vertex sign invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Model positions as graph vertices/edges, assign ±1 to edges and vertices depending on state, and show the total product is invariant under allowed local operations; use parity of initial product to contradict final state's product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: removal/flipping game where deleting a vertex and flipping neighbors negates some signs; show overall product P unchanged, compare initial and final P to obstruct full removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gcd / invariant count of odd common divisors under transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show certain operations preserve the number of odd common divisors (or the set of odd divisors), thereby restricting possible gcd outcomes to powers of 2 or other constrained forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transformations preserve number of odd common divisors implying gcd(x,y) must be a power of 2; use minimality or descent arguments to establish reachability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose invariants tailored to combinatorial token-passing games
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the 'current value' sum modulo n or use signing arguments to track fixed residues; these invariants detect impossibility of evenly-distributed final states or infinite termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in card-passing games, S = sum of card-values modulo 1994 remains invariant, preventing desired final distribution; signing cards shows 'stuck' cards between neighbors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit rapidly-growing sequences to cover ranges in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Define sequences like a_{k+1}=a_k(a_k−1) that grow quickly so showing f(m)=m for m ≤ a_k eventually covers all integers as k→∞, enabling global induction after establishing small base cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to extend local equalities to all integers by proving f(n)=n up to arbitrarily large bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce Diophantine equations to Pell equations by completing the square
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate given Diophantine equalities (multiply, complete square) to obtain equations of the form X^2 − dY^2 = ±1 (Pell or negative Pell), which can be analyzed with standard methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out multiplications by suitable constants, complete the square, and identify X and Y substitutions (e.g., 2n+1 and 2k+1) to arrive at Pell equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate Pell solutions from fundamental unit / use (u+v√d)^k
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the fundamental solution (x1,y1) of x^2 − d y^2 = 1 (or −1) and raise (x1 + y1√d)^k to produce infinite families; extract explicit formulas or recurrences for solution sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide closed forms like x_k + y_k√d = (x1 + y1√d)^k and use parity/odd-even indices to pick solutions matching original parity constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity and congruence constraints on Pell solutions to satisfy original conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every Pell solution corresponds to the original problem; impose additional parity or mod constraints (e.g., x odd/even, y multiple of 4, index even) to select valid solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: require xn even or residues modulo 4 to match derived substitutions; use residues mod small primes to derive divisibility (e.g., n divisible by 40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage quadratic residues modulo small primes to obtain divisibility restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze congruences modulo small primes (2,3,5,8, etc.) and quadratic residue sets to deduce necessary divisibility properties of unknowns (e.g., n ≡ 0 mod 8 and mod 5 ⇒ n divisible by 40).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine residues modulo different primes to force divisibility by their product when compatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose Pell solutions to build new solutions (multiplicative composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use composition formulas: if (x1,y1) solves x^2 − d y^2 = A and (x2,y2) solves same type, suitable bilinear combinations give solutions to products of right-hand-sides (useful to build solutions of x^2 − d y^2 = ab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: produce x= x1x2 + d y1y2 and y = y1x2 + x1y2 to solve x^2 − d y^2 = (x1^2 − d y1^2)(x2^2 − d y2^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pell solutions to produce factorial-divisibility examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose n from Pell or negative Pell solutions large enough so that certain prime-power factors appear in n! and hence force divisibility properties like n^2 + 1 | n!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pick n solving n^2 − 5m^2 = −1 with n large so that 5m^2 divides n! and conclude n^2 + 1 divides n!.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Lucas’s theorem to binomial coefficients modulo prime p
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Lucas’s theorem: binomial(n,k) ≡ ∏ binomial(n_i,k_i) (mod p) where n_i,k_i are base-p digits; a coefficient is 0 mod p iff some k_i>n_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count non-multiples of p by taking product (n_i + 1) over base-p digits; deduce number of binomial coefficients divisible by p is (n+1) − ∏(n_i+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count odd binomial coefficients via binary expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: A central binomial coefficient C(n,k) is odd iff the set of 1-positions in binary of k is a subset of those in n; hence number of odd coefficients is 2^{(# of ones in binary n)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct application of Lucas’s theorem with p=2; useful for combinatorial parity problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count coefficients with specified residues modulo small primes by digit combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: For modulus 3 (or other small primes), express n in base 3, partition digit positions into sets A (digits 1) and B (digits 2), and count k choices digitwise to tally coefficients congruent to 1 or 2 mod 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform combinatorial sum over allowable digit choices (ki ≤ ni) and parity constraints on digits in B to obtain explicit counts (e.g., difference equals 2^r where r = count of digits equal to 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elementary binomial expansions and numerator/denominator considerations for congruences mod p^2
rubrics_metrics.description: When Lucas’s theorem no longer applies (mod p^2), expand factorial ratios and use p-adic valuation/induction to derive congruences like binomial(np,p) ≡ p n^{p−1} (mod p^2) phenomena or related congruences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with m=0 base case and proceed by induction, analyze numerator/denominator factors modulo p^2 and use that denominators are not divisible by p to control congruence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurrence relations from Pell / unit powers to deduce divisibility/limit properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Express sequences of solutions by linear recurrences derived from powers of fundamental units and use these recurrences to show growth, divisibility, or gcd properties (e.g., an→∞ so an−1 divides b_n^2 etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret matrices or closed forms to extract asymptotics and divisibility conclusions, often used in Putnam/USAMO-level arguments.
